To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the escape rate is given by the inverse of the time that the particle needs to overcome the barrier in a single escape attempt.

(i) the time‐dependent reaction rate is determined by the escape probability from the metastable state, which is the solution of an initial value problem; (ii) the time‐averaged escape probability is determined by the time‐dependent escape probability, which is the stationary solution of a nonlinear, nonlocal, partial differential equation.

(i) the rate of escape from metastable potentials is strongly enhanced in the case of periodically driven noise, and (ii) the enhancement of the rate is a universal function of a dimensionless control parameter, the driving frequency, and the barrier width of the potential.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of a periodically driven, damped, inertial particle moving in a metastabile, piecewise parabolically shaped potential.
the dynamics of a damped and driven Brownian particle in an external potential.
the study of the influence of thermal noise on the escape of a damped, driven particle out of an oscillating potential.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our method provides a reliable, accurate, and efficient way for the determination of reaction rates in multidimensionally driven escape problems.
the path integral method is a very efficient and reliable tool to determine the time‐dependent and the time‐averaged escape rate in multidimensional systems.
the present method is a powerful tool for the analysis of the activated escape of a particle over oscillating barriers, in particular for the situation where the barrier is not symmetric.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a method for the calculation of time‐averaged rates in multidimensional escape problems, which is valid for all frequencies and all damping strengths.
the method presented here allows for a systematic study of multidimensional escape problems at low noise levels.
we have developed a general method for the calculation of escape rates in multidimensional systems with oscillating barriers at weak thermal noise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the presence of inertia, activated escape over oscillating potential barriers can be described by the same effective potential as that for escape over a static barrier.
the rate of activated escape is determined by the average time the particle spends in a metastable well.

, in contrast to the case of one dimension, the time‐averaged escape rate is not simply given by the product of the average of the escape rate and the period of driving, but is instead given by the average of the product of the escape rate with the period.
